findings.headline: Concessionary Fares saving not agreed with local transport authority, flagging future overspend
findings.detail: The council planned to save £35k on tramway concessionary fares through revised capping, but the saving was not agreed with the local transport authority. The council explicitly states that an overspend will occur in future years as a result, to be covered by the service.
findings.matters: An unresolved structural overspend that will impact future budget balance. The explicit acknowledgment that the overspend 'will be covered by the service' indicates a known but unmitigated cost pressure with no clear resolution.
findings.figures: £35k planned saving not achieved; £35k future overspend flagged
findings.quote: Overspend will occur in future years, to be covered by the service

findings.headline: Children's Services external placement reduction strategy did not deliver expected cost savings
findings.detail: The council aimed to reduce high-cost external placements by increasing lower-cost internal foster care. However, internal placements increased without corresponding decreases in external placements, reducing the net savings. The children's services directorate achieved only 73% of its £1.980m savings target.
findings.matters: Children's services is typically high-cost and growing. A failed cost-control strategy indicates forecasting or execution risk in a key spending area, suggesting the council may not deliver on future savings plans.
findings.figures: Children's Services unachieved savings £530k (73% achievement rate)
findings.quote: Although Internal Foster Care Placements increased, external fostering placements didn't decrease at the same rate.

findings.headline: CQC inspection diverted focus from £1.7m of Adult Services cost-reduction initiatives
findings.detail: Three Adult Services initiatives targeting £3.726m in savings were significantly undermined by the CQC inspection, which diverted council focus and operational resources. Only £1.991m were achieved, with £1.735m unachieved across strengths-based assessment, single-handed care, and daycare services. These unachieved savings were built into the 2026/27 MTFP.
findings.matters: Shows that external regulatory pressures can override financial recovery plans. An inspection finding indicates underlying service issues that could worsen the financial position in a typically high-cost and growing service area.
findings.figures: Adult Services target £3,726k, achieved £1,991k, unachieved £1,735k (47% miss)
findings.quote: Initial reviews yielded some savings in this area, however, focus was diverted after receipt of the CQC inspection report.

findings.headline: Budget savings delivery achieved only 71%, with £2.5m shortfall and unachieved items deferred to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council planned £8.647m in service savings for 2025/26 but achieved only £6.114m, resulting in a £2.533m shortfall (29% of target). The paper shows that unachieved savings were built into the 2026/27 MTFP, meaning future years start with the same recovery challenges and may face additional pressure.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can execute its financial recovery plan. A 71% achievement rate indicates execution risk, and carrying unachieved savings forward annually compounds structural deficit pressure.
findings.figures: Target £8,647k, Achieved £6,114k, Unachieved £2,533k (29% shortfall)
findings.quote: Total Savings Proposals 8,647 6,114 2,533

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves have declined by £7.7m and are being consumed by service deficits faster than they can be replenished
findings.detail: Available earmarked reserves fell from £33.9m to £26.3m in a single year, mainly because Growth/Prosperity and Leisure deficits were transferred into reserves to isolate them from the operating budget. This is accounting, not recovery — the deficits are still there.
findings.matters: Earmarked reserves are being used to hide operating deficits rather than as a buffer for genuine contingencies. If two major service areas (Leisure, Growth schemes) continue to overspend, reserves will be exhausted within a few years.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £33.920m (2024-25) to £26.265m (2025-26); decline of £7.656m
findings.quote: Members are asked to note that the level of available earmarked reserves has decreased by £7.656m from £33.920m to £26.265m during 2025/26. The main reasons for the decrease in reserves are due to an increase in the Growth and Prosperity deficit and receipt of government grant monies late in 2024/25 which have been used in 2025/26.

findings.headline: DSG deficit has tripled to £7.3m and depends on a government grant that expires in 2028
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit accumulated over three years to £7.331m. The council is forecasting a High Needs Stability Grant will pay 90% of this, leaving £0.733m that must be funded from the council's own resources by 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: This is a time bomb. The council has three years to find £0.733m (minimum) from operational budget or reserves to close a SEND cost overrun it cannot control. If Special Education Needs demand continues to grow, the residual could be much larger.
findings.figures: DSG deficit grew from £2.295m to £7.331m in one year; forecast residual liability £0.733m after grant
findings.quote: To which the in-year overspend for 2025-26 of £5.523m was added, and then Safety Valve income of £0.470m was deducted, along with other minor adjustments. As at the 31st of March 2026, the cumulative deficit stands at £7.331m. Subject to DfE acceptance of Blackpool's SEND Reform Plan in 2026-27, the High Needs Stability Grant will be paid, which will reduce the overall deficit by 90%. The Council is forecasting a Cumulative Deficit that needs to be funded of £0.733m after the grant, but before any net over or under spend from 2026-27 is brought in.

findings.headline: Parking income target missed by £1.55m, a critical shortfall in a commercialised service
findings.detail: Parking overspent by £1.872m, with £1.551m of that due to income falling short of target. This is not a cost overrun; it is a revenue failure in a service the council is running as a commercial operation to fund other services.
findings.matters: If parking is not generating expected income, it casts doubt on the commercial case for other council enterprises. This matters to a lender because it shows the council may be overestimating income-earning capacity.
findings.figures: Parking overspend £1.872m; income shortfall £1.551m
findings.quote: Parking was £1,872k overspent. This was mainly due to insufficient income to meet the income target (£1,551k).

findings.headline: Council Tax collection is the 4th worst in England and arrears are growing sharply
findings.detail: Collection rate fell to 90%, against a target of 97.5%. Arrears have risen from £29.6m to £33.4m year-on-year. Bad debt provision increased from £12.54m to £14.73m. The council notes this reflects 'the current economic climate', meaning the problem is getting worse, not stabilising.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the largest controllable income stream. A 4th-worst collection rate means this council faces structural income loss, not a temporary dip. Rising arrears imply more households unable to pay, foreshadowing further shortfalls.
findings.figures: Collection rate 90% vs 97.5% target; arrears £33.4m (was £29.6m); bad debt provision £14.73m (was £12.54m)
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026 the level of arrears has increased to £33.4m (compared to £29.6m in 2024/25) and the provision for bad debts has increased to £14.73m (compared to £12.54m in 2024/25). These reflect the current economic climate and the risks associated with the Council Tax Reduction Scheme.

findings.headline: £2.5m (29%) of planned budget savings failed to materialise
findings.detail: The council targeted £8.647m in savings for 2025-26. It achieved £6.114m, leaving £2.533m unachieved. This is not a small miss; it represents a systemic failure to deliver nearly a third of intended cost reductions.
findings.matters: If 29% of savings are unachievable, future spending plans that rely on savings will also fail. This creates recurring deficits that must be covered by reserves or one-off assets sales.
findings.figures: Target savings £8.647m; achieved £6.114m; unachieved £2.533m
findings.quote: At its meeting on 24 February 2025 Council agreed to budget savings of £8.647m in 2025/26. Appendix 2n shows the savings achieved in 2025/26 of £6.114m with savings not achieved of £2.533m.

findings.headline: General Fund working balances have fallen to £325k against a £7.4m target — a 96% shortfall
findings.detail: The council ended the year with only £325k in liquid reserves, then immediately added £6.9m from the new-year budget to reach £7.225m. This one-shot transfer masks the underlying position: the council ran the year with almost no reserve cover and has no buffer for unforeseen costs.
findings.matters: Working balances are the council's emergency fund. At £325k against a £211m budget, this council has almost zero resilience to a single bad decision or unexpected cost. A lender needs to see whether the £6.9m injection for 2026-27 is sustainable or just deferring a crisis.
findings.figures: Target £7.4m; actual 31 March 2026 £325k; restocked to £7.225m on 1 April 2026
findings.quote: The Council's Revenue Budget for 2025/26 set a target level of General Fund working balances of around £7.4m by 31 March 2026. The level of working balances as at 31 March 2026 is forecast to be £325,000.

findings.headline: Strategic Leisure Assets deficit has grown to £12.8m; borrowing costs exceed income
findings.detail: A £1.75m overspend in 2025-26 added to £11m carried forward. The core problem is that income from leisure operations does not cover the borrowing charges and repairs needed to run the facilities. This is a structural mismatch, not a one-off pressure.
findings.matters: Leisure assets are funded by prudential borrowing that is not serviced by the activity. The deficit is growing, not shrinking. Future overspends will either drain reserves or require subsidy from rates and council tax.
findings.figures: £1,752k overspend 2025-26; cumulative deficit £12,780k
findings.quote: Strategic Leisure Assets (Appendix3) had a pressure of £1,752k. This is due to the income generated not being sufficient to cover the borrowing as well as repairs and other costs incurred by the service.

findings.headline: Growth and Prosperity regeneration schemes have accumulated an £11m deficit and are not meeting their business cases
findings.detail: In-year overspend of £5.9m added to a carried-forward £5.2m deficit. The council notes that 'the bulk of the pressure relates to schemes not meeting their business case expectations'. They are now relying on an Asset Disposal Strategy to recover the losses, which is still in 'mature form' but not yet delivering.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether these are temporary timing issues (income delayed) or structural failures in project economics. The council's recovery plan is asset-dependent, which creates refinancing risk if property sales slow.
findings.figures: £5,133k in-year overspend on schemes; cumulative deficit now £11,053k
findings.quote: This left a pressure of £5,133k relating to Growth and Prosperity schemes. Some pressure was expected due to the projects being regeneration in nature. The bulk of the pressure relates to schemes not meeting their business case expectations. The Growth and Prosperity team are currently working on reducing this figure to ensure that losses are recovered in future years and reserves replenished with an Asset Disposal Strategy, now in a mature form, integral to this.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care placement costs running £7.7m over budget with no cap in sight
findings.detail: Residential placements hit 76 against a forecast of 62. The overspend is driven by new admissions exceeding exits and additional support costs following placement breakdowns. This is structural — the council budgeted for fewer children in care than were actually placed.
findings.matters: Demand-led spend that the council cannot control or predict. If the pattern continues, this £7.7m overspend will repeat in 2026-27 and must be accommodated in future budgets or absorbed from reserves.
findings.figures: £7,712k Children's Social Care overspend; 76 placements vs 62 forecast
findings.quote: There was an overspend on Children's Social Care of £7,712k, mainly due to new-to-care placements being higher than those exiting care and the additional support required following the breakdown of high-cost placements. The actual number of residential placements as at 31 March 2026 was 76 with an original forecast of 62.

findings.headline: Treasury Management revenue overspend of £830k against budget
findings.detail: Treasury costs ran £830k over budget (£27.5m actual vs £26.7m budgeted). The shortfall was driven by £392k in lower-than-expected HRA recoverable interest and £588k in loans interest receivable that fell short due to specific loans being renegotiated at year-end.
findings.matters: Higher treasury costs than forecast reduce the council's financial headroom and indicate either forecasting weakness or changing market conditions materializing mid-year.
findings.figures: £27,496k actual vs £26,666k budget (£830k overspend); £392k HRA shortfall; £588k interest receivable shortfall
findings.quote: The Treasury Management revenue account for 2025/26 had net expenditure of £27,496k against the budget of £26,666k. The HRA recoverable interest was less than expected in 2025/26 leading to a £392k pressure in year. There was also a shortfall of £588k in the loans interest receivable due to specific loans being re negotiated at year-end.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement Limit and Long-Term Liabilities Limits exceeded
findings.detail: Blackpool exceeded both its Capital Financing Requirement Limit and Long-Term Liabilities Limits in 2025/26. The overage in the CFR was driven by additional loans taken in-year, reduced business loan repayments, and additional capital spending funded through prudential borrowing. The liabilities limit was exceeded due to PFI accounting reclassifications moving items from Right of Use Assets to Long-Term Liabilities.
findings.matters: Prudential limits are the statutory framework controlling council borrowing capacity. Exceeding them signals the council has borrowed more than its Medium-Term Financial Plan anticipated and constrains future borrowing headroom.
findings.figures: CFR Limit exceeded; Long-Term Liabilities Limits exceeded
findings.quote: Capital Financing Requirement Limit was exceeded in 2025/26 due to additional loans given in 2025/26, a reduction in the repayments expected from business loans in 2025/26 and additional capital expenditure in year funded through prudential borrowing. The Long-Term Liabilities Limits were also exceeded in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Eleven priority 1 audit recommendations from 2025/26 remain unimplemented
findings.detail: High-priority audit findings across multiple areas remain unimplemented, including creditors financial control (2), cyber security back-up and detection (2), Growth and Prosperity Medium Term Financial Plan (1), business planning (1), contract management (1), and others. These are being monitored quarterly but their continued non-implementation extends exposure to identified risks.
findings.matters: Unimplemented priority 1 recommendations indicate the council is not promptly addressing high-risk audit findings. Extended remediation timelines increase exposure to these risks and may reflect organisational implementation challenges.
findings.figures: 11 priority 1 recommendations outstanding across multiple service areas
findings.quote: There are a number priority one recommendations made in 2025/26 which have still not been signed off as completed by the Head of Audit and Risk

findings.headline: Resource constraints and loss of organisational knowledge driving increase in limited audit findings
findings.detail: The number of limited or split assurance statements has increased during 2025/26. Internal audit attributes this to reducing resources, loss of organisational knowledge, and lack of service and medium-term planning in some areas. This indicates staffing pressures are impacting the council's ability to manage risks.
findings.matters: Resource constraints and knowledge loss suggest the council lacks sufficient capacity to manage operations effectively. This compounds financial sustainability concerns and may impact the council's ability to maintain financial control.
findings.figures: Increase in limited or split assurance statements attributed to staffing reductions and knowledge loss
findings.quote: The assurance work undertaken during the year has identified an increase in the number of limited or split assurance statements issued where the root cause can be attributed to reducing resources, loss of organisational knowledge and a lack of service / medium term planning in some areas.

findings.headline: Internal audit identified key weaknesses in financial systems and processes
findings.detail: Audit work revealed weaknesses in the council's financial systems and processes that require strengthening. This indicates gaps in the systems that manage and control financial transactions, recording, and reporting across the organisation.
findings.matters: Weaknesses in financial systems represent control gaps that could lead to errors or mismanagement of council finances. This directly impacts the reliability of financial information and the council's ability to manage resources effectively.
findings.figures: Key weaknesses identified in unspecified financial systems
findings.quote: Internal audit work also identified key weakness in some financial systems and processes which need to be strengthened in order improve the control environment.

findings.headline: Auditor gives limited assurance on financial sustainability, identified as the council's greatest risk
findings.detail: The Head of Audit and Risk has issued limited assurance specifically on financial sustainability, driven by increasing demand for social care and various large-scale regeneration projects. This is compounded by a qualified external audit opinion on the 2024/25 accounts, which limits the council's ability to evidence robust financial stewardship and rebuild assurance.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on financial sustainability is a direct red flag for lenders assessing creditworthiness. The qualified external audit opinion on prior accounts indicates historical financial reporting issues requiring attention.
findings.figures: Limited assurance rating on financial sustainability; qualified external audit opinion 2024/25
findings.quote: However, the Head of Audit and Risk provides limited assurance with regards to financial sustainability which is the greatest risk faced by the Council with the increasing demand for social care and the various large scale regeneration projects. It is difficult to evidence robust financial stewardship due to a qualified external audit option for the 2024/25 accounts limiting the Council's progress to build back assurance.

findings.headline: Increase in limited assurance audit statements due to resource constraints and knowledge loss
findings.detail: The number of limited or split assurance statements from internal audit has increased. The root causes are identified as reducing resources, loss of organisational knowledge, and lack of service/medium term planning in some areas.
findings.matters: An increase in limited assurance indicates deteriorating control environments across multiple council services; combined with resource constraints, this signals reduced capacity to manage financial and operational risks.
findings.figures: Increase in limited assurance statements during 2025/26
findings.quote: The assurance work undertaken during the year has identified an increase in the number of limited or split assurance statements issued where the root cause can be attributed to reducing resources, loss of organisational knowledge and a lack of service / medium term planning in some areas.

findings.headline: Director of Finance position vacant; recruitment underway during period of financial stress
findings.detail: The council is actively recruiting to fill the vacant Director of Finance position. This represents a gap in senior finance leadership during a critical period when financial systems are weak, accounts are unaudited, and social care demand is increasing.
findings.matters: The Chief Finance Officer is responsible for statutory financial management and reporting. Vacancy during a period of audit weakness and financial sustainability concerns creates additional governance risk.
findings.figures: Director of Finance recruitment target: September 2026
findings.quote: Recruit to the vacant Director of Finance position. We are doing this to ensure that there is adequate capacity in the Corporate Leadership Team

findings.headline: Internal audit identified key weaknesses in financial systems and processes requiring strengthening
findings.detail: Internal audit work has identified weaknesses in financial systems and processes that need to be strengthened to improve the control environment. This contributes to the difficulty in evidencing robust financial stewardship.
findings.matters: Weak financial systems increase risk of error, fraud, and unreliable financial reporting; they are foundational to effective financial management and control.
findings.figures: Not quantified in document
findings.quote: Internal audit work also identified key weakness in some financial systems and processes which need to be strengthened in order improve the control environment.

findings.headline: Head of Audit provides limited assurance on financial sustainability, identified as the council's greatest risk
findings.detail: The Head of Audit and Risk has given limited assurance on financial sustainability due to increasing social care demand and large-scale regeneration projects. Weakness is compounded by the qualified 2024/25 external audit opinion, making it difficult to evidence robust financial stewardship.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on financial sustainability directly threatens the council's ability to meet its financial obligations; this is the core concern for lenders to local government.
findings.figures: Social care demand increasing; £90 million for housing regeneration announced
findings.quote: However, the Head of Audit and Risk provides limited assurance with regards to financial sustainability which is the greatest risk faced by the Council with the increasing demand for social care and the various large scale regeneration projects. It is difficult to evidence robust financial stewardship due to a qualified external audit option for the 2024/25 accounts limiting the Council's progress to build back assurance.

findings.headline: External auditors unable to form full opinions on council accounts; unmodified opinion not expected until 2026/27 audit
findings.detail: The 2024/25 accounts were signed with a disclaimed opinion due to national audit capacity constraints. Due to significant issues raised, the council will not receive unmodified account opinions until the 2026/27 audit is completed. This limits assurance on the accuracy and completeness of the council's financial statements.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audited accounts to understand a council's true financial position; disclaimed or modified opinions indicate unresolved accounting issues and create uncertainty about reported figures.
findings.figures: 2024/25 accounts have significant issues; 2026/27 is the target for first unmodified opinion
findings.quote: However, it will be the 2026/27 accounts audit before members will receive accounts that have an unmodified opinion as we follow the government prescribed process for building back External Audit reassurance not withstanding the significant issues raised in the 2024/25 accounts.

findings.headline: Loan amount and affordability assessment withheld from publication.
findings.detail: Appendix 8a containing loan terms, interest rate, and business plan assessment is exempt under Schedule 12A. Council states this is to avoid undermining its negotiating position.
findings.matters: The actual loan-to-value ratio and affordability metrics are not disclosed, preventing external assessment of lending discipline and terms.
findings.figures: Loan amount: undisclosed
findings.quote: The Loan terms at Appendix 8a are exempt from publication by virtue of Paragraph 3 of Part 1 of Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act 1972

findings.headline: Council deploying capital through Business Loans Fund into property-backed lending; second tranche to Damexa.
findings.detail: This is a follow-on to a smaller loan issued February (decision PH9/2026). Damexa is refurbishing derelict properties for rental and serviced accommodation. The new loan is secured by first charge over existing rented properties. Damexa operates 50 rental properties and 12 serviced accommodation units and has been trading 5 years.
findings.matters: Shows Blackpool is deploying capital into commercial real estate lending, creating credit exposure and concentration risk to a single borrower across multiple tranches.
findings.figures: £7.1m property security; Damexa has 50 rental properties and 12 serviced accommodation properties
findings.quote: supported by a first charge over existing rented properties with a value of £7.1m

findings.headline: Earmarked Revenue Reserves declining to £19.18m, at or near minimum policy levels with no buffer for future pressures
findings.detail: The paper notes that Earmarked Revenue Reserves are forecast to reduce to £19.18m by 31 March 2026 'as existing commitments unwind'. A graph shows these have returned to pre-COVID and pre-austerity levels. The council sets a local target minimum of £18.0m for ERR, so at £19.18m there is only minimal headroom. These reserves provide the only buffer for multi-year budget pressures.
findings.matters: Depleted earmarked reserves mean the council has limited ability to smooth multi-year pressures or fund invest-to-save initiatives. Any major unbudgeted commitment will require service cuts.
findings.figures: Earmarked Revenue Reserves: £19.18m forecast at 31 March 2026; local minimum target: £18.0m; headroom only: £1.18m
findings.quote: Earmarked Revenue Reserves are forecast to reduce to £19.18m as at 31 Marh 2026 as existing commitments unwind.

findings.headline: Interest rate risk: if PWLB rates rise above the 4.04% assumption, higher borrowing costs will squeeze revenue budget within already tight cash limits
findings.detail: The treasury budget assumes an average interest rate of 4.04% based on Office of Budget Responsibility forecasts. However, the paper flags 'material risk' from global economic volatility and uncertainty around future rate direction. Sensitivity analysis shows that a 1% rise in rates costs an additional £2.027m, and a 2% rise costs £5.044m. The council's policy of a 50:50 split between short and long-term borrowing only 'partially mitigates' this risk.
findings.matters: With capital commitments made and no flexibility in reserves, a rate spike could create a sudden revenue shortfall that forces emergency action. This is an exogenous risk the council cannot control.
findings.figures: Assumed average rate: 4.04%; cost of 1% rate rise: £2.027m; cost of 2% rise: £5.044m
findings.quote: Potential impacts on the Council are higher than expected borrowing costs, particularly through the PWLB, would increase the revenue required to support the Capital Programme. This introduces a risk of a financial "squeeze" should borrowing assumptions need to be revised in-year.

findings.headline: Pay award budget assumes 2.2%, but a 1% overshoot costs £1.2m and would force immediate corrective action with minimal working balance headroom
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget assumes a 2.2% pay award. The council notes that a 1% movement equals approximately £1.2m in cost. Given the lack of working balance headroom (only £6.919m) and the need to hold that as a buffer, 'any increase above the planning assumption would require immediate compensating action or further recurrent savings'. This creates salary negotiation pressure and inflation sensitivity.
findings.matters: With minimal reserves and tight cash limits, the council has no flexibility on pay negotiations. Any public sector pay award above 2.2% could force emergency cuts to services mid-year.
findings.figures: Pay award assumption: 2.2%; cost of 1% variance: ~£1.2m; working balances only: £6.919m
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget assumes a 2.2% pay award. For context, the 2025/26 budget assumed a 2.6% award at a cost of approximately £3.2m, and a 1% movement equates to around £1.2m. Given the lack of headroom in working balances, any increase above the planning assumption would require immediate compensating action or further recurrent savings.

findings.headline: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 provides only £14.5m uplift (6.6%), of which 39% is self-generated council tax, leaving underlying challenge unresolved
findings.detail: Government's new funding formula was supposed to better recognise deprivation and redistribute resources. Blackpool receives £14.5m growth (6.6%) in 2026-27, but £5.7m (39%) must come from council tax rises. Over the three-year settlement, council tax will account for 59% of growth. The CFO explicitly states this 'does not address the depth of deprivation locally nor resolve the Council's underlying funding challenge'.
findings.matters: The new settlement falls short of recognising Blackpool's structural funding challenge. The council must rely on tax rises rather than grant growth, limiting fiscal room and raising political and social resistance to affordability.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power uplift: £14.5m (6.6%); self-generated from Council Tax: £5.7m (39%); over 3-year period: 59% from Council Tax
findings.quote: Although the reforms are intended to better recognise need and redistribute resources towards more deprived areas, the estimated uplift for Blackpool is only around £14.5m (6.6%) in 2026/27 of which £5.7m (39%) is self-generated from Council Tax, and this increases to 59% over the 3-year settlement period. This does not address the depth of deprivation locally nor resolve the Council's underlying funding challenge.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements at 76 and growing, with pressures also from SEN transport demand exceeding budget assumptions
findings.detail: Month 9 monitoring shows 76 residential placements driving overspends in both volume and cost. Additionally, rising Education, Health and Care Plans are putting pressure on home-to-school transport, requiring £1.6m growth in the 2026-27 budget. Despite this growth allocation, the paper flags continued EHCP growth as a 'significant risk'. Children's Social Care now represents 32% of the council's net revenue spend (17% in 2011-12).
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand that the council's largest and fastest-growing cost driver (social care) is driven by demand the council cannot control and is consistently overshooting budget. This is structural, not cyclical, and shows no sign of stabilising.
findings.figures: 76 residential placements at Month 9; Children's Social Care 32% of net revenue (2026-27) vs 17% in 2011-12; £1.6m growth in home-to-school transport
findings.quote: At Month 9 there were 76 residential placements, with overspends driven by both the number and cost of placements, as well as pressures in education transport and related services.

findings.headline: The Chief Finance Officer warns of Section 114 risk if budget conditions are not met
findings.detail: The CFO (Section 151 Officer) states 'The Council's financial resilience remains fragile' and delivers an explicitly cautious professional opinion. The budget is 'only just robust' and reserves 'only just adequate' conditional on four specific requirements being met. Failure to deliver would create risk of requiring 'Exceptional Financial Support or consideration of a Section 114 notice' — a formal notification that expenditure exceeds resources.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a serious governance failure that triggers government intervention. This warning is the CFO's professional red flag that without very tight execution, the council could enter financial crisis.
findings.figures: Section 114 threshold: when expenditure exceeds available resources
findings.quote: The Council's financial resilience remains fragile... Failure to deliver these conditions would materially increase the risk of requiring Exceptional Financial Support or consideration of a Section 114 notice.

findings.headline: Working balances are critically depleted at £0.019m at end of current year, far below the £7.0m minimum policy
findings.detail: Month 9 forecast for 2025-26 shows the council will draw down £7.39m from working balances to cover in-year overspends, leaving balances at only £19k. Although a planned transfer of £6.9m will reinstate balances to £6.92m, this still leaves the council with almost no safety margin below its target of £7.8m, and the CFO explicitly states reserves are 'only just adequate'.
findings.matters: Working balances this tight mean the council has almost zero capacity to absorb any unexpected shock or shortfall. This is the single most important indicator of financial vulnerability for lenders assessing credit risk.
findings.figures: Unallocated working balances: £0.019m at 31 March 2026 (vs £7.0m minimum); after transfer: £6.919m (vs £7.8m target)
findings.quote: Unallocated General Fund working balances are forecast to be £0.019m at 31 March 2026, significantly below the Council's current minimum policy level of £7.0m. However, a transfer of £6.9m as at 1 April 2026 will reinstate these to £6.919m.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit will reach £13.53m by March 2027, with the statutory override ending in 2028 leaving an unfunded liability
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grows by £7.87m in 2026-27 due to rising Education, Health and Care Plans demand with no additional High Needs funding from government. The statutory override allowing the deficit off the balance sheet expires in March 2028, after which the council must fund this or find alternative solutions. The paper notes the County Councils Network projects national SEND deficits will reach £17.8bn by 2029.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that Blackpool faces a structural liability that will hit the balance sheet in two years, with no clear funding source or national policy direction.
findings.figures: £7.87m in-year deficit in 2026-27; cumulative deficit £13.53m by 31 March 2027; statutory override ends 2028
findings.quote: The estimated in-year deficit generated is £7.87m after forecasting for these, which in turn increases the cumulative deficit on the Dedicated Schools Grant to £13.53m by 31 March 2027. Whilst this an extremely difficult position to face, the Government is due to publish a White Paper on SEND Reform

findings.headline: Council lacks financial capacity for new long-term investment and is under-borrowing by £183.7m
findings.detail: The strategy states the council 'does not currently have significant levels of funds for long-term investment' and therefore does not invest in property solely for financial returns. As of 31 March 2026, the council under-borrows by £183.7m, using reserves and working capital instead of borrowing, indicating constrained financial capacity.
findings.matters: A council that lacks capacity for new investment and uses reserves to reduce borrowing has limited financial flexibility to respond to income shocks or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing: £183.7m; revenue budget: £217.62m
findings.quote: As the Council does not currently have significant levels of funds for long-term investment, the Council does not invest in property as an Investment Strategy solely to achieve financial income.

findings.headline: Council budget depends critically on £7m commercial rental income; without it, services would be cut
findings.detail: The strategy states that the council has maintained service activity 'through use of the income generated from investments in group companies and strategic commercial income,' and that 'Without this income services would have had to be reduced at a time when they are most needed.' Commercial rental income of £7m represents 3.09% of the 2026/27 budget of £226.327m.
findings.matters: The council's ability to meet financial obligations depends on commercial property income, not just statutory funding. Market downturn or property vacancy could force budget cuts or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Commercial rental income 2026/27: £7m; net service expenditure: £226.327m; proportion: 3.09%
findings.quote: The Council has only been able to maintain and increase service activity and support to the local community in recent years through use of the income generated from investments in group companies and strategic commercial income. Without this income services would have had to be reduced at a time when they are most needed as other support for the vulnerable in Blackpool is under severe pressure.

findings.headline: £111.2m loan portfolio faces elevated risk of non-repayment due to economic pressures on borrowers
findings.detail: The council has made loans to various entities including Blackpool Housing Company (£40.4m) and Blackpool Transport Services (£19.6m). The strategy explicitly acknowledges that economic uncertainties and inflation will likely impact these borrowers' ability to repay loans in 2026/27, with monthly monitoring and recovery actions planned.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's exposure to businesses struggling with repayment. Default by major borrowers would create liquidity pressure and force recovery actions.
findings.figures: Total loans £111.2m; largest loans: Blackpool Housing Company £40.4m, Blackpool Transport Services £19.6m, Coolsilk £11.6m
findings.quote: The current economic uncertainties as a result of inflationary pressures and other external factors beyond the council's control are likely to continue to have an impact on businesses in 2026/27 and their ability to repay loans drawn down.

findings.headline: Adult and children's services targeting £2m savings through demand management and placement mix changes
findings.detail: The council is planning £1m in adults services demand management (including removal of mileage allowance in supported living fees) and £1m in children's services commissioning and placement mix reductions. These are demand-led, vulnerable service areas where budget cuts may affect service users.
findings.matters: Changes to adult and children's services commissioning can indicate pressure on vulnerable populations and risk creating future liabilities if unmet need materialises; finance directors must assess sustainability.
findings.figures: £1,000k adults commissioning demand management; £1,000k children's services commissioning and placement mix; £300k adults fee rate changes
findings.quote: Children's Services - Commissioning 1,000 Demand Management and placement mix

findings.headline: £1.5m of savings dependent on commercial income increases, heavily weighted to tourism-related discretionary revenue
findings.detail: Blackpool is targeting £1.5m in additional commercial income (20% of total savings), including increases from Blackpool Tourism Limited. This is discretionary, non-recurring revenue dependent on visitor numbers and business performance, not a controllable cost reduction.
findings.matters: Lenders prefer savings from cost control; reliance on discretionary commercial income exposes the budget to volatility if tourism demand weakens or businesses underperform.
findings.figures: £1,500k planned commercial income increase
findings.quote: Place - Commercial 1,500 Increase in commercial income to the Council directly and indirectly from Blackpool Tourism Limited

findings.headline: Employer pension contributions cut from 11.4% to 9.0%, saving £2m but deferring long-term liabilities
findings.detail: The council is reducing employer pension contributions by 260 basis points to achieve £2m in savings—26% of total savings proposals. This decision follows a Pensions Committee meeting on 23 January 2026. Reducing pension funding rates defers costs rather than eliminating them, increasing future liabilities.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders track pension obligations as a liability. Underfunding pensions to meet current year deficits increases future contribution requirements and signals use of accounting measures rather than real cost control.
findings.figures: £2,000k saving; contribution rate reduction from 11.4% to 9.0%
findings.quote: Corporate - Pension contributions 2,000 Further reduction in Employers pension contributions from 11.4% to 9.0% following Pensions Committee on 23rd January

findings.headline: Working balances depleted; council deploying £6.9m release to replenish reserves to £6.919m
findings.detail: The council is using a £6.9m provision set aside for replenishment to restore working balances to £6.919m at 1 April 2026. This indicates the council has already drawn down its financial reserves to cover previous deficits and lacks a buffer for unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves signal reduced financial resilience; low working balances limit the council's capacity to absorb cost pressures or revenue shortfalls without further borrowing.
findings.figures: £6,900k provision release; £6,919k forecast working balances at 1 April 2026
findings.quote: Top up to Working Balances 2026/27 6,900 Release of provision set aside to replenish depleted working balances

findings.headline: £4.966m remaining budget gap to be met from flexible use of capital receipts strategy, not sustainable revenue savings
findings.detail: After identifying £7.5m of savings proposals against a £12.5m adjusted budget gap, Blackpool still faces an unresolved deficit of £4.966m. The council plans to cover this through 'applying the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy'—a one-off measure that treats capital resources as revenue funding. This indicates the council cannot balance its budget through operational improvements alone.
findings.matters: Lenders assess sustainable revenue generation; funding a structural deficit from capital receipts indicates diminishing capital resources and reliance on one-off measures rather than structural solutions.
findings.figures: £15,901k original budget gap; £12,466k adjusted gap; £7,500k savings; £4,966k unresolved gap
findings.quote: 2026/27 Budget Gap / (Surplus) 4,966 To be met from applying the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy

findings.headline: Interest rates above 3% continue to constrain capital scheme affordability despite recent rate cuts
findings.detail: While falling interest rates have reduced pressure from 2025, rates remaining above 3% still create 'considerable pressure' on capital schemes. Capital spending is often financed through internal balances and short-term loans.
findings.matters: Even with recent Bank of England rate cuts (base rate now 3.75%), the council's capital programme remains financially constrained; indicates limited headroom in affordability.
findings.figures: Base rate cut from 4.5% (April 2025) to 3.75% (Dec 2025); rates assumed above 3% in 2026
findings.quote: With interest decreasing in 2026 some of the pressure applied in 2025 has reduced, however with interest rates remaining at above 3% there is still a considerate pressure being applied to capital schemes.

findings.headline: Capital regeneration programme continues to rely on borrowing rather than central government grants
findings.detail: Central government capital grants remain at a low level, and the council is funding its capital regeneration through borrowing. Major schemes including Talbot Gateway Phase 5 and the Multiversity project are continuing, with total annual cash flow expected to exceed £1.5 billion.
findings.matters: Creates long-term debt servicing obligations for regeneration projects rather than grant-funded delivery; lenders need to understand the council's structural dependence on debt markets.
findings.figures: Over £1.5 billion annual cash flow; multiple ongoing regeneration schemes
findings.quote: Capital grants received from central government remain at a low level but the Council is using borrowing to invest in regeneration. Total cash moving annually through the Council's bank account including the re-investment of temporary cash surpluses and re-borrowing of temporary cash shortfalls is expected to once again be over £1.5 billion in the current year.

findings.headline: Council has shifted to longer-term borrowing to hedge against economic uncertainty
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Panel has deliberately increased longer-term borrowing in 2025/26 to maintain a 50:50 split between long-term and short-term debt. This strategic shift is explicitly stated as a hedge against economic uncertainty around interest rates and gilt yields.
findings.matters: Shows the council recognizes refinancing risk and is managing its debt maturity profile defensively; affects the sustainability of its borrowing costs and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 50:50 split target; 10-year gilt yields 4.45-4.75% (down from peak in Jan 2025); short-term borrowing rate assumed at 4.04% in 2026
findings.quote: Consequently, the Treasury Management Panel has decided to take some 'shorter-end' long-term borrowing in 2025/26 to regain the 50:50 split between long-term and short-term borrowing as a hedge to the economic uncertainty.

news_drafts.headline: Concessionary Fares saving not agreed with local transport authority, flagging future overspend
news_drafts.lead: An unresolved structural overspend that will impact future budget balance. The explicit acknowledgment that the overspend 'will be covered by the service' indicates a known but unmitigated cost pressure with no clear resolution.

news_drafts.headline: Children's Services external placement reduction strategy did not deliver expected cost savings
news_drafts.lead: Children's services is typically high-cost and growing. A failed cost-control strategy indicates forecasting or execution risk in a key spending area, suggesting the council may not deliver on future savings plans.

news_drafts.headline: CQC inspection diverted focus from £1.7m of Adult Services cost-reduction initiatives
news_drafts.lead: Shows that external regulatory pressures can override financial recovery plans. An inspection finding indicates underlying service issues that could worsen the financial position in a typically high-cost and growing service area.
